query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing about 5 atomic percent tungsten (W) into the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its dynamic strain hardening and uniform deformability under adiabatic high-rate loading. This modification is expected to delay the onset of adiabatic shear banding by enhancing dislocation storage and increasing phonon drag, thereby increasing the dynamic yield strength, extending uniform plastic deformation, and boosting impact-induced energy absorption relative to the baseline properties.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA with quasi‐static properties: yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and fracture strain of 13.5%.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by substituting approximately 5 atomic percent tungsten (W) in place of part of Ta to form a modified HfZrTi(Ta,W)0.53 composition.
generation.conditions: Dynamic deformation under adiabatic conditions at high strain rates (approximately 1000–3000 s⁻¹) using compression tests (e.g., split-Hopkinson pressure bar experiments), with direct comparison to quasi-static and baseline dynamic behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening from W addition, which promotes a finer dispersion of dislocations and possible formation of (or improvement in) secondary nanostructural features that impede dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten atoms, due to their high melting point and larger atomic size, increase the resistance to dislocation glide by boosting forest dislocation interactions and phonon drag effects at high strain rates. This delays dislocation mobility and the nucleation of adiabatic shear bands, thereby extending uniform deformation and increasing energy absorption during impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to show an increase in dynamic yield strength by roughly 10–20% over 786 MPa, improved strain hardening leading to a greater uniform deformation strain (beyond 13.5%), enhanced resistance to adiabatic shear localization (fewer and delayed shear bands), and a higher impact-induced energy release compared to the baseline alloy under high strain-rate loading.
generation.baseline: The unmodified HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy with quasi‐static yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and 13.5% fracture strain.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies to adiabatic dynamic deformation conditions at strain rates in the range of roughly 1000–3000 s⁻¹. Effects may not be significant under quasi‐static loading or at temperatures where thermal activation dominates over phonon drag.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvements are approximate and dependent on processing routes and microstructural evolution; the optimum W content and its distribution may require further refinement. Variability in dynamic test conditions could also influence the degree of enhancement observed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical thermomechanical processing: one set of the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy and a second set where approximately 5 at.% tungsten is substituted for part of the Ta. Subject both sample sets to dynamic compression tests using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar at strain rates of 1000, 2000, and 3000 s⁻¹. Compare the dynamic yield strength, strain-hardening rate, uniform deformation (plastic strain before localization), incidence of adiabatic shear banding, and energy absorption during impact loading.
measurements: Uniform plastic strain (percentage prior to localization)
Frequency and morphology of adiabatic shear bands (via post-mortem microscopy)
Impact-induced energy release (quantified by energy absorption metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (≥10% increase) in dynamic yield strength, enhanced uniform ductility, higher strain hardening, and reduced or delayed shear localization compared to the baseline alloy under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity.
